text:
NFL 🏈
Regular Season | Week 1

New York Giants vs. Dallas Cowboys

The first Sunday Night Football game of the season features two teams with very different realities. The Giants have spent several years unsuccessfully searching for a competitive roster. They have failed to do so, leaving them in the shadow of division rivals such as the Philadelphia Eagles and the Cowboys themselves. They invested heavily in quarterback Daniel Jones for a long time, but he failed to live up to the challenge. Today, the New York team begins the season with young quarterback Jaxson Dart leading the offense. After 12 starts, he finished his first season in the league with a 4-8 record.

The Cowboys, on the other hand, have a roster with much greater ambitions than their opponent tonight. They have had quarterback Dak Prescott leading an offense featuring several high-level players for years. Defensively, they are no slouches either; they are a well-balanced team in all aspects of the game. In recent years, Dallas has not had many problems during the regular season. However, it is in the postseason where they have failed to perform at the expected level.

Home-field advantage carries significant weight in the NFL. But we do not believe that factor will be enough for the Giants to prevail tonight. Dallas, a much more established team, should be able to use its experience to impose its quality and come away with the victory.

Prediction:
Dallas Cowboys to win
Odds: 1.58

Thoughts?

text:
THE ARIK MATSON SURVIVOR STORY
January 6th, 2020

It was a sleepy Monday night in Waseca, Minnesota, when Officer Arik Matson and his fellow officers responded to a suspicious-person call—the kind of call most cops take hundreds of times throughout their career.  Nothing about it suggested how profoundly that night would change their lives. On January 6, 2020, Arik was shot in the line of duty, a painful reminder that no call is ever truly routine for law enforcement.

Arik survived, but survival was only the beginning. The injury changed nearly every part of his life, and the road through treatment and rehabilitation demanded more than most of us can imagine. Through it all, his love for his two daughters and his determination to remain present in their lives as their dad gave him a reason to keep pushing forward.

In this episode, Arik, the three fellow officers who were there that night, his mom, and his brother help tell his story. The photos and videos on Arik’s story page offer another glimpse of the officer, father, family, and community behind it. We hope you’ll spend a few minutes looking through them, then listen to The Arik Matson Story, a special edition of the Officer Down Memorial Podcast available Wednesday morning.

https://t.co/xibZIeHUNS

Thank you to our friends and partners at Law Enforcement Labor Services, Inc. For sponsoring this amazing story.

text:
Glioblastoma lives by growth signals that should have been switched off. Ohio State researchers asked how those signals stay on when protein phosphatase 2A, an enzyme that normally damps them, is still present in the cell. The answer they offer is a set of endogenous inhibitors, SET among them, along with ANP32A and CIP2A, that hold PP2A back.

John Ryan Jacob and colleagues report in Cancer Letters that knocking those inhibitors down restored phosphatase activity, disrupted oncogenic kinases, and cut tumor formation in preclinical models. SET loss was the starkest result: in intracranial xenografts, tumors failed to appear. Silencing the same proteins also left DNA-damage kinases ATR and ATM more open to PP2A, which in the laboratory made cells worse at repairing radiation injury and holding a cell-cycle checkpoint.

That is a mechanism, not a medicine. The work is in cells and animals. Stopping a graft from taking is not the same as clearing a tumor already growing in a human brain, and no one yet knows whether the pathway can be blocked in patients without harming the tissues that also use PP2A. The modest claim is still useful. A cancer that shrugs off radiation and chemotherapy may do so in part by sitting on its own brakes. If those brakes can be released, existing treatment might finally have something to work against.

[Jacob, J. R., Nimjee, S. M., Elder, J. B., Chakravarti, A., & Palanichamy, K. (2026). Endogenous inhibitors of PP2A activate oncogenic and DNA damage response kinases in glioblastoma. Cancer Letters, 645, 218325. DOI: 10.1016/j.canlet.2026.21832
